title: Query complexity of Max-CSP testing
formal: Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), the randomized query complexity \(q_{D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s}(n)\) of distinguishing bounded-degree constraint instances with optimum satisfied fraction at least \(c\) from those with optimum at most \(s\). The target ranges over every fixed finite predicate template \((D,\Gamma)\), degree bound \(d\), density lower bound \(\alpha\), and gap \(0\le s<c\le1\), under the variable-query model defined below. Taking \(\alpha=0\) includes unrestricted bounded-degree inputs; positive \(\alpha\) includes the source’s density-bounded model.

source_formulation.text: Determine the query complexity of \(MaxCSP(\Gamma )[c, s]\) in the bounded-degree model, for all predicate families \(\Gamma\) and parameters c and s.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 6

why: This asks for a general account of how much of a sparse constraint system must be inspected to distinguish high from low optimum value. It covers different predicates, value gaps and densities in one query model, and could identify broad structural boundaries between local testing and essentially complete inspection. Its complexity bounds are information-based and need not assume computational hardness conjectures.
status_note: Checked on 14 September 2026. The 2026 published primary source retains the full query classification as Question 13. category_assignment.reason: The target is bounded-degree oracle query complexity for distinguishing Max-CSP value gaps, which is explicitly a property-testing task.

importance.reason: A broad structural classification problem across finite CSP templates and approximation gaps in a central sublinear-query model. It connects local access to global optimization and contrasts constant, intermediate and linear inspection costs, with meaningful links to streaming approximation beyond a single predicate or parameter improvement.

sentences: A tester must distinguish constraint systems whose optimum satisfied fractions lie on opposite sides of a fixed gap.
It can query variables to reveal incident constraint occurrences, with only a constant number of occurrences per variable.
The target is the asymptotic query complexity for every finite predicate template, gap, degree bound and density regime.
The actual number of constraints matters because value is normalized by constraints rather than by all possible incidence slots.
Known linear lower bounds and related streaming results leave the complete query classification unresolved.

definitions: The domain \(D\) is a nonempty finite set, and \(\Gamma\) is a finite collection of predicates \(R:D^{k_R}\to\{0,1\}\), with positive integer arities \(k_R\). A predicate is specified by its full finite table and ordered coordinates; these tables are fixed parameters known to the tester. For an integer \(n\ge1\), an instance has variable set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and a finite multiset \(\mathcal C\) of \(m\) constraint occurrences. An occurrence consists of a predicate \(R\in\Gamma\) and an ordered tuple of \(k_R\) distinct variable labels. Identical occurrences may be repeated and each copy is counted separately. The degree of a variable is the number of occurrences containing it. Fix an integer \(d\ge0\) and a real \(\alpha\in[0,d]\); admissible instances have maximum degree at most \(d\) and \(m\ge\alpha n\). Thus \(\alpha=0\) permits empty or very sparse instances, while \(\alpha>0\) enforces a linear number of constraints. For an assignment \(\tau:[n]\to D\), an occurrence \((R,(v_1,\ldots,v_{k_R}))\) is satisfied when \(R(\tau(v_1),\ldots,\tau(v_{k_R}))=1\). If \(m>0\), define \[\operatorname{val}(I)=\frac{1}{m}\max_{\tau:[n]\to D}\sum_{(R,\mathbf v)\in\mathcal C}R(\tau(v_1),\ldots,\tau(v_{k_R})).\] Put \(\operatorname{val}(I)=1\) when \(m=0\). Fix real constants \(0\le s<c\le1\). YES instances have \(\operatorname{val}(I)\ge c\), NO instances have \(\operatorname{val}(I)\le s\), and no correctness condition is imposed between the two thresholds. The tester knows \(n,D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s\), but receives neither the constraint list nor its actual length \(m\). A query specifies a variable \(v\in[n]\). If an as-yet-unrevealed constraint occurrence involving \(v\) exists, the oracle reveals one such occurrence, giving its predicate and full ordered variable tuple. Otherwise it returns \(\bot\). Revealing an occurrence marks that copy as seen globally, including at its other variables. Distinct identical copies remain distinct possible future responses. Which available occurrence is returned may be chosen adversarially as a function of past queries and replies, subject to one fixed input instance; the oracle cannot depend on unrevealed future random choices. Every oracle call, including one returning \(\bot\), costs one query. Arbitrary variable labels may be queried without first being discovered. Local computation, storage and private random choices are free; there is no direct uniform-constraint sampling oracle, no degree oracle and no free inspection of \(m\). Query complexity is defined by finite randomized adaptive decision trees: finite probability distributions over deterministic query-and-answer trees, with rational probabilities, whose leaves output accept or reject. Each deterministic tree can choose its next variable from the preceding transcript. No time, space or tree-size bound is imposed. A tester is valid if it accepts every YES instance and rejects every NO instance with probability at least \(2/3\), for every valid oracle response policy. Its cost is the maximum number of queries on any branch. Let \(q_{D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s}(n)\) be the minimum integer cost of a valid tester. If one promise side is empty, including when no admissible instance exists, this minimum can be zero. All parameters in the subscript are held fixed as \(n\) grows; they are not growing input-length parameters. A matching asymptotic classification must retain their effects on which growth regime occurs.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct characterization checked in Lean of the asymptotic query growth for all fixed parameter tuples in the definition. In particular, specify nonnegative comparison functions \(f_{D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s}(n)\), with corresponding upper and lower bounds, such that for each fixed tuple some constants \(A,B>0\) and \(n_0\) satisfy \[A f_{D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s}(n)\le q_{D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s}(n)\le B f_{D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s}(n)\qquad(n\ge n_0).\] Constants may depend on the fixed tuple, but not on \(n\), the instance or the oracle order. Zero-query cases must be correctly included. The classification need not consist of a prescribed finite list of cases, but it must establish growth rates rather than merely rename or repeat the defining decision-tree optimization. Polylogarithmic gaps between upper and lower bounds do not meet the requested constant-factor precision. Results only for perfect completeness \(c=1\), one template, a special gap, or a positive-density subclass do not cover the full target. A streaming-space or polynomial-time approximation classification is not a query classification.

context_blocks.text: A Max-CSP instance asks for an assignment satisfying as many local predicates as possible. A query tester is allowed to inspect only selected incident constraints and must distinguish two separated ranges of the optimum value, even though it has unlimited ability to process what it has seen.

The fraction satisfied is normalized by the actual number of constraint occurrences. This differs from ordinary bounded-degree property-testing distance, which counts edits relative to the degree bound times the number of variables. The difference matters when most variables are isolated.

Fei therefore introduces \(\mathrm{BD}^{*}(d,\alpha,n)\), requiring at least \(\alpha n\) constraints for fixed positive \(\alpha\). The present density parameter includes both that model and \(\alpha=0\), the original bounded-degree regime. It keeps the sparse-instance issue visible rather than silently assuming linear density.

Question 13 asks for the complexity of all predicate families and completeness–soundness pairs. This card makes the degree, density and oracle conventions explicit and chooses constant-factor matching bounds as its asymptotic acceptance precision. No claim is made that a previously proved dichotomy already supplies those bounds.

Even the perfect-completeness satisfiability setting displays several behaviors. The source surveys constant-query languages, square-root lower bounds with nearly matching upper bounds for graph bipartiteness, and linear lower bounds for graph 3-colorability. These examples do not classify every imperfect-completeness gap.

Fei’s Theorem 8 proves a linear lower bound at some fixed gap, degree and positive density for every unbounded-width template. Here bounded width means that some fixed level of local consistency suffices to decide satisfiability for all instances; unbounded width means that no such fixed level suffices. The theorem does not determine the optimal hardness gap or the growth at all other parameter choices.

Fei, Minzer and Wang’s April 2026 preprint strengthens related streaming lower bounds and extends the unbounded-width obstruction to that model. Its Section 1.4 explicitly still refers to the full query-complexity question as unresolved. The streaming results therefore provide relevant progress without completing the requested query classification.

Reading the entire bounded-degree instance gives a linear-query upper bound for fixed degree, irrespective of local computation time. The substantive issue is which templates and value gaps allow substantially less inspection and what the precise intermediate rates are.
